nodes.title: Context Scaling: A New Frontier of AI Scaling
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.33160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context a...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.33160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many failures of deployed AI arise not from weak inference but from a mismatch between the state a task depends on and the context available when the system acts. Relevant user state, repository revisions, tool traces, sensor readings, or environment changes may be unavailable, distorted, or poorly selected. We call the effort to reduce this bottleneck context scaling. We frame a model as $P_\theta(d\mid c)$ within a system governed by three budgets: training $B_\theta$, decision-time $B_d$, and context-infrastructure $B_c$. Pretraining scaling invests in $\theta$; decision-time scaling searches, refines, or verifies decisions under supplied context; context scaling improves the system's capacity to acquire, represent, deliver, evaluate, and persist deployment state for model use. The three programs interact, but only $B_c$ targets what the system can make available before a decision. This view makes the model-infrastructure pair the unit of analysis. We define effective-context value as a task- and intervention-dependent attribution, separate deployment state from model-visible context, and identify availability, fidelity, selection, and utilization failures. We then organize current mechanisms through a five-operation context lifecycle and propose controlled budget interventions and utility-cost curves for evaluation. The resulting agenda centers on grounded reporting, interaction-data and full-cost infrastructure, and safety and governance for persistent, adaptive systems.

nodes.title: Constraint-Aware Test-Time Scoring for LLM and VLM Candidate Selection
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.33161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned ...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.33161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM or VLM produces several candidate answers, picking the best one usually relies on the model's own confidence, a learned judge model, or a domain check. Each has a known weakness: an answer can be fluent but insecure, mathematically plausible but physically infeasible, or rated highly by a judge while quietly breaking a task requirement. We propose a scoring framework that combines a small set of hard checks every answer must pass with a wider set of softer checks whose scores are blended into one number per candidate. This adaptive scoring framework consists of three components: a drafting model that produces the candidates, a configuring model that selects and weights the checks for each task, and scoring models that rate properties no grounded tool can compute. We apply our proposed method to four tasks: writing code that is both correct and secure (CWEval), generating robot manipulation plans (LIBERO with added safety variants), passing competitive-programming hidden tests (LiveCodeBench), and answering questions from retrieved documents (HotpotQA). An ablation study isolates the contribution of each component and finds that the largest gains come from combining hard checks with candidate comparison: on tasks where the first sampled answer is often broken or unsafe, this pairing lifts joint correctness-and-safety by up to +0.21 (retrieval-augmented QA) and code-generation safety by up to +0.28 (CWEval), with the size of the gain tracking how weak the first sample is, falling to near zero or slightly negative where it is already strong. The per-task layer that selects and weights the softer checks adds no measurable value over simpler alternatives. This builds a unified scoring framework, together with an ablation that identifies the grounded hard checks, not the soft-factor configuration, as the source of the gain.

nodes.title: AutoformBench: A Lean Formalization Benchmark for Advanced Mathematics
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.33165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical for...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.33165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI systems are increasingly capable of producing machine-checked Lean proofs of advanced mathematical results. Real mathematical formalization, however, is not isolated theorem proving: it requires building the definitions and intermediate lemmas that connect a result to a formal library. Existing evaluations often provide isolated theorem statements in settings where much of this supporting theory is already available in Mathlib. We introduce AutoformBench, a benchmark of 341 Lean 4 formalization tasks drawn from 24 advanced mathematical sources. Lean-experienced mathematicians formalized and audited each target statement, leaving the corresponding Lean proof to the evaluated agent. Each problem is embedded in a broader mathematical development: agents receive the informal proof but must translate it into Lean while constructing the missing definitions, intermediate lemmas, and supporting infrastructure. We compare the performance of frontier models on these problems. We find a largely shared difficulty frontier: success depends less on mathematical domain than on models' ability to construct missing formal infrastructure. Data and code at https://github.com/facebookresearch/autoformbench

nodes.title: General-Purpose Decision Models for AI Configuration Tuning
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.33190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.33190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI configuration tuning searches for settings that improve the performance of AI systems under a limited budget. Existing tuners use different sampling and search policies, making the choice of decision strategy central to both tuning quality and cost. We investigate whether general-purpose decision models can guide tuning, using Jev as a deployed representative that returns structured choices and numeric scores across diverse tasks. To assess where it helps, we compare its use as an optimizer, performance predictor, and region guider against conventional methods and a large language model (LLM) on eight AI tuning tasks. Conventional optimizers attain rank 1 in six of eight comparisons. Similarly, established predictors outperform Jev in seven. Through region guidance, however, it finds configurations with lower perplexity than those selected by the native tuner, offering a quality gain when additional decision time and API fees are acceptable. These findings yield actionable recommendations on selecting the decision role, retaining conventional predictors, and balancing tuning quality against cost.

nodes.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.33263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models pr...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.33263v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.

nodes.title: CISA Adds 10 Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
nodes.tldr: CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path ...
nodes.details: CISA has added 10 new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2023-25914 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Path Traversal Vulnerability CVE-2023-25915 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Input Validation Vulnerability  CVE-2025-41450 Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series Improper Authentication Vulnerability  CVE-2026-103406 Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) Juniper Session Smart Conductor and Session Smart Router OS Command Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-133275 Mitel MiCollab Unrestricted Upload of File with Dangerous Type Vulnerability  CVE-2026-133303 Mitel MiCollab XML Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-133311 Mitel MiCollab Weak Authentication Vulnerability  CVE-2026-133323 Mitel MiCollab OS Command Injection Vulnerability  CVE-2026-133324 Mitel MiCollab Not Failing Securely Vulnerability  CVE-2026-133469 Vates Xen Orchestra Improper Validation of Specified Type of Input Vulnerability  These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

nodes.title: AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software
nodes.tldr: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow attackers to corrupt application memory and cause instability or a crash, potentially leading to arbitra...
nodes.details: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow attackers to corrupt application memory and cause instability or a crash, potentially leading to arbitrary code execution, if a user is convinced to open a malicious file. The following versions of AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software are affected: C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80 (CVE-2026-127280) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.8 AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software 1 Vulnerability Heap-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing, Energy, Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-127280 C-More EA9 Programming Software V6.80 does not adequately validate data read from a project file before using it in heap memory operations. A crafted file causes a heap buffer overrun during file open, resulting in heap corruption and instability within the application. An attacker can exploit this vulnerability by convincing a user to open a malicious project file delivered through common distribution channels such as email, file sharing, or removable media. Read More 1 Affected Product AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software <=V6.80 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate C-More EA9 Programming Software to V6.81: https://www.automationdirect.com/support/software-downloads MitigationIf you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment. Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-122 Heap-based Buffer Overflow CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.8 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 8.4 HIGH CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:A/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments rgod of TrendAI Zero Day Initiative reported this vulnerability to CISA.   Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. nodes.details: View CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges. The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected: AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 (CVE-2026-129713) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 9.8 Danfoss AK-SM8xxA 1 Vulnerability Stack-based Buffer Overflow Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial Facilities Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Company Headquarters Location: Denmark Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-129713 A stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability. Read More 1 Affected Product Danfoss AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 Product Status: known_affected Remediations MitigationThis vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases. MitigationUntil a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overview Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-121 Stack-based Buffer Overflow CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 9.8 CRITICAL CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H 4.0 9.3 CRITICAL CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Carlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. nodes.title: Commission proposes Quantum Act and new Sovereign Tech Equity Fund to strengthen Europe's industrial
nodes.tldr: Commission proposes Quantum Act and new Sovereign Tech Equity Fund to strengthen Europe's industrial capacity and security Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/25/2026 - 08:52 The Euro...
nodes.details: Commission proposes Quantum Act and new Sovereign Tech Equity Fund to strengthen Europe's industrial capacity and security Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/25/2026 - 08:52 The European Commission today proposed the Quantum Act, a new framework to help turn Europe's quantum research into products and services, strengthen supply chains and prepare Europe's digital systems for post-quantum cryptography. GettyImages © AliseFox The proposal also lays the groundwork for the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF). The impact of quantum technologies will be profound, from navigation without satellites and faster drug discovery to ultra-advanced batteries and next-generation secure communications. Quantum technologies are moving from laboratories to products and services. The Quantum Act has three main pillars: research excellence, bringing quantum technology into use, and keeping systems and supplies secure. These will be delivered through the Quantum Europe Framework Initiative, which will bring together EU and national programmes around shared priorities for research and industry. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: "Quantum technologies will shape the future of industry, security and innovation, and they will have a profound impact on our societies. Europe needs to accelerate now. With the Quantum Act, we are putting in place the key elements to turn our world-class quantum research into industrial capacity, strengthen critical supply chains and prepare for the cyber risks linked to quantum computing. Europe has already built strong foundations in quantum; now we must turn them into industrial scale, resilient supply chains and secure deployment." nodes.title: European Digital Infrastructure Consortium launches today to strengthen digital sovereignty in educa
nodes.tldr: European Digital Infrastructure Consortium launches today to strengthen digital sovereignty in education Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/20/2026 - 11:30 Today, the European Commis...
nodes.details: European Digital Infrastructure Consortium launches today to strengthen digital sovereignty in education Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/20/2026 - 11:30 Today, the European Commission and eight Member States are launching the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC) to pool resources and develop shared, secure and interoperable digital infrastructure and services for education. GettyImages © anyaberkut The new consortium on education brings together Belgium, Croatia, Finland, France, Greece, Slovenia, Spain and the Netherlands, which will be hosting the EDIC. The initiative will strengthen Europe's technological resilience while making high-quality digital tools accessible to schools, teachers and learners. It will also help narrow the digital divide in education by supporting solutions that can be used across national education systems, regardless of their resources or technological capacity. Today's launch marks an important milestone in fostering innovation and excellence in education and contributing to the EU's technological sovereignty ambitions. Executive Vice-Presidents Henna Virkkunen and Roxana Mînzatu, together with Judith Tielen, Minister for Primary and Secondary Education of the Netherlands, will welcome the launch. Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, said: “Today's launch of the European Digital Infrastructure Consortium on Education is an important step towards achieving Europe's technological sovereignty in one of our most sensitive and strategic sectors. Education shapes our future, and Europe must be able to rely on trusted, safe and interoperable digital solutions that reflect European values and principles. By working together with the Member States, we can build a resilient European digital education infrastructure that supports learners, educators and schools across the Union.” Roxana Mînzatu, Executive Vice-President for Social Rights and Skills, Quality Jobs and Preparedness, said: “Recently, we officially launched the Education and Skills Package and announced the establishment of the EDU-EDIC consortium. Today, we are reiterating our commitment to reinforce education for Europe's future. Our priority is to ensure that education is ready for the AI era. We will work together with Member States to pool expertise in strategic areas such as cloud infrastructure, AI for education, secure data exchange across educational institutions, and Europe's education technology (EdTech) sector.” You can also read more about other European Digital Infrastructure Consortium (EDIC). Related topics Creating a digital society Digital skills Europe's Digital Decade European Digital Infrastructure Consortium Technological sovereignty Related content News article20 November 2026Member States join forces to develop sovereign digital infrastructure on educationEight EU countries join forces to develop trusted, accessible digital education services and strengthen digital sovereignty.

nodes.details: Commission hosts Apply AI Summit to boost Europe’s AI innovation and uptake Anonymous (not verified) Mon, 11/16/2026 - 13:43 Nearly 1,000 high-level policymakers, start-ups, industry leaders and researchers will take part in the Apply AI Summit in Brussels tomorrow. They will discuss how artificial intelligence (AI) can boost Europe’s competitiveness across 10 strategic sectors and the public sector. The summit will also showcase concrete AI applications, European success stories and innovative projects.  Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, will host the summit and present the first Apply AI Startup Award to three European start-ups. The award recognises innovative European startups and scaleups developing AI solutions in the strategic sectors. Alongside the in-person event, an online conference platform will run from 16 to 20 November, allowing additional 2,500 participants to join part of the summit. The Apply AI Summit marks one year since the adoption of the Apply AI Strategy, which sets out how to speed up the use of AI in Europe’s key industries and the public sector. It concludes the first European AI Innovation Month, running from 14 October to 17 November 2026, organised by the European Commission in partnership with the Irish Presidency of the Council of the European Union. nodes.tldr: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The Euro...
nodes.details: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures.
